title: Talli
pitch: A conversational credit ledger that helps small businesses and their AI agents manage customer debt together, without taking financial control away from the human.
about_excerpt: A conversational credit ledger that helps small businesses and their AI agents manage customer debt together, without taking financial control away from the human. Like Comment Story Updates Talli helps small businesses and informal traders record and manage customer credit using ordinary speech, text, or Telegram. Instead of filling out accounting forms, a merchant can simply say, “Adele took goods worth $40 and will pay on Friday,” or “She paid $10 today.” Talli turns those conversations into structured customer balances and transaction histories. Through WebMCP, a browser agent can securely read the same live ledger, answer questions, identify overdue debts, and prepare proposed financial updates. However, the agent cannot finalize those changes. The merchant reviews and confirms every consequential update inside Talli’s visible interface. The Problem Millions of small businesses and informal traders sell goods on credit every day. A customer may take food, clothing, supplies, or other goods and promise to pay later. The business owner needs to remember: who took the goods how much they owe when they promised to pay whether they made a partial payment how much remains outstanding which customers are overdue Many business owners manage this information using paper notebooks, memory, calculator notes, chat messages, or a mixture of all four. This creates serious problems. Records can be lost, payments may not be reflected correctly, and business owners can struggle to explain how a customer’s balance was calculated. When several customers have similar names, it is also easy to update the wrong person’s record. Traditional accounting applications can help, but they are often designed around forms, tables, categories, and bookkeeping terminology. For someone who is busy serving customers and may not consider themselves an accountant, recording a simple credit transaction can feel like administrative work. The real challenge is not that these business owners do not understand their businesses. The challenge is that most financial software does not work the way they naturally communicate. The Solution Talli is a conversational credit ledger built around the way small businesses already talk about customer debt. Instead of completing a long form, a merchant can speak or type naturally: “Adele took goods worth $40 and will pay next Friday.” Talli converts that statement into a structured financial record containing the customer, amount, currency, transaction type, and relevant date. Later, the merchant can say: “Adele paid $10.” Talli records the partial payment, updates Adele’s outstanding balance, and preserves the history of how that balance changed. The merchant can also ask questions such as: “How much does Adele still owe?” “Who owes me money?” “Which payments are overdue?” “Show me Adele’s transaction history.” “How much have my customers paid?” “Mark this debt as settled.” Talli supports voice, typed conversations, a web interface, and Telegram. The same underlying ledger can therefore remain useful while the merchant moves between the channels they already use. Talli also understands that financial records require caution. If a request is unclear, Talli does not silently guess. It asks for clarification before allowing the wrong customer or obligation to be changed. The WebMCP Extension For the WebMCP Challenge, I extended Talli so that the live website can expose its financial capabilities directly to browser-based AI agents. Without WebMCP, an agent trying to assist a Talli user would have to inspect the page, interpret text on the screen, locate buttons, fill forms, and simulate clicks. That approach is fragile and can be especially dangerous when the website contains financial information. With WebMCP, Talli explicitly tells the agent what it can do, what information each operation requires, and which operations are read-only. The agent can discover structured tools for searching customers, checking balances, reviewing histories, finding overdue debts, and preparing ledger changes. It receives structured results from the same live ledger the person is viewing. This creates a shared workspace between the merchant, the browser agent, and Talli. A Typical Human-Agent Workflow Imagine that a merchant asks their browser agent: “Check Talli and tell me how much my customers owe me.” The agent calls Talli’s get_ledger_summary tool and receives a structured summary from the current ledger. The merchant then says: “Adele paid $10. Update her balance.” The agent calls prepare_ledger_mutation , but Talli discovers that several customers match the name “Adele.” Instead of choosing one, Talli returns clarification_required with a short list of matching customers and their balances. The ledger remains unchanged. The agent can then ask: “I found more than one Adele. Which customer made the payment?” After the merchant identifies the correct customer, the agent prepares the payment again. Talli validates the request and displays a visible review card containing the exact proposed change. The merchant reviews the amount and customer, then clicks Confirm inside Talli. Only at that point does the ledger change. This workflow demonstrates more than an agent operating a website. The agent helps with interpretation and preparation, Talli enforces financial safety, and the human retains final authority. Why Talli Is a Strong Fit for WebMCP Talli is a strong WebMCP use case because customer credit management combines repetitive work with consequential financial decisions. An AI agent is well suited to: searching records summarizing balances finding overdue obligations reviewing transaction histories translating a natural-language request into a structured proposal However, an agent should not silently make an irreversible or incorrect financial change. WebMCP provides the structured boundary Talli needs. It allows the agent to interact with the application through clearly defined tools instead of guessing its way through the interface. Talli builds on that boundary with three important rules: Read operations can happen directly. Financial mutations must first become proposals. Only the human can confirm a proposal in Talli’s visible interface. The most important behavior is not simply that Talli knows how to act. It also knows when not to act. If two customers match a name, an obligation cannot be safely identified, or the ledger has changed since a proposal was prepared, Talli pauses the operation instead of guessing. This makes WebMCP part of the product’s safety model, not just another way to call backend functions. How Talli Creates a Better User Experience Talli reduces the amount of effort required to maintain accurate credit records. The merchant does not need to learn database fields, accounting terminology, or a complicated menu system. They can continue communicating naturally while Talli and their agent handle the structured work underneath. WebMCP improves this experience in several ways: The agent can access reliable structured data instead of trying to read values from the visual interface. The merchant can ask broader questions without manually searching through individual customer records. The agent can prepare a transaction while the merchant remains focused on running the business. Ambiguous requests produce clarification instead of silent errors. Proposed financial changes are shown in a visible, understandable review card. The merchant keeps control over the final decision. The agent and the person work from the same current ledger rather than separate or outdated copies of the data. Talli remains usable in browsers that do not support WebMCP. WebMCP is added as a progressive enhancement, so the normal voice, text, web, and Telegram experiences continue to work. What People and Agents Can Do Together That Was Difficult Before Before the WebMCP extension, Talli could already understand conversations and maintain the ledger. However, an external browser agent did not have a dependable, structured way to use those capabilities. Now a person and their agent can work together to: inspect the business’s total outstanding credit search for a customer without manually navigating the interface explain how a customer’s current balance was calculated identify overdue obligations prepare new credit, payment, or settlement entries detect ambiguous customer references ask the human to resolve uncertainty present the exact financial change for review prevent an agent from confirming its own proposal keep a record unchanged until the human explicitly approves it For example, the agent can do the time-consuming work of finding the correct records and preparing an update, while the business owner makes the final judgment. That division of responsibility was difficult to achieve reliably through ordinary browser automation. WebMCP makes it possible to define the collaboration explicitly.
